Bright light early in the day is the strongest cue your body clock gets. It keeps your rhythm anchored, so sleepiness shows up on time tonight and mornings feel easier. We time it from when you usually wake, because watch data can take a while to arrive.

Caffeine fades slowly: hours after your last cup, much of it is still at work. Stopping about 10 hours before bed gives it time to wear off, so it doesn\'t make sleep harder to start or shallower once it does.

A big meal keeps digestion busy and warms you up, and both get in the way of settling into deep sleep. Finishing heavy meals about 3 hours before bed lets things calm down. A light snack later is fine.

A drink can make you feel drowsy, but alcohol breaks sleep up later in the night and leaves less of it restful. Leaving about 3 hours between your last drink and bedtime gives your body time to clear it.

Moving during the day helps you sleep, but a hard session late keeps your heart rate and body temperature up. Finishing intense workouts about 2 hours before bed leaves time to cool down. Gentle stretching is fine any time.
Bright evening light tells your body it\'s still daytime and holds sleepiness back. Turning down lamps and screens as your wind-down starts lets your natural night-time signals build.
A short, familiar routine tells your mind the day is over. Pick a few easy things you enjoy and start them as your wind-down begins, so drifting off comes more naturally.

Your target bedtime sits in the middle of your best window for falling asleep, worked out from your rhythm and sleep need. Getting into bed now makes it easier to drift off and helps you pay down sleep debt.
Energy naturally sags in the early afternoon, which makes it the easiest time to nap. Keep it to 10–20 minutes so you wake up refreshed and still sleep well tonight.
